item.title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
item.description: Jim LaValle reveals how the gut-immune-brain interface drives chronic inflammation, and why stress, blood sugar and environmental toxins play key roles.
item.content:encoded:
Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health.

Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.

Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection.

LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response.

Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation.

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle.

He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated.

Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said.

This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut."

ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS

"So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people.

Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health.

Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted.

Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes.

Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said.

Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle.

LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.

The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health.

LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added.

Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well."

Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.

item.title: A child's question at a funeral reminded us death does not get the last word
item.description: A five-year-old's question at his great-grandmother's funeral sparked reflections on C. S. Lewis, hospice hymns, and the hope of eternity.
item.content:encoded:
The question came unexpectedly from my five-year-old grandson.

My late mom’s pastor had gathered our family to explain how her funeral service would go and asked if we had any final questions before we processed into the church.

Raising his hand, my grandson inquired, "Will we see Momma Bettie again?"

DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME

The poignancy of his request brought tears to the eyes of almost everyone in the room.

As I pondered seeing my mom again in heaven, my grandson’s query brought to mind C. S. Lewis’s famous sermon, "The Weight of Glory." Given at Oxford in 1941, Lewis posed the thought-provoking statement, "There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal."

This Christian belief — that we are both image-bearers of God and have eternal existence — was the basis from which Lewis preached. And for followers of Jesus — he provided an eternal perspective — not only that our life has purpose and a higher calling, but how we should truly love those around us.

As Lewis concluded his sermon, "Next to the Blessed Sacrament itself, your neighbour is the holiest object presented to your senses. If he is your Christian neighbour he is holy in almost the same way, for in him also Christ vere latitat — the glorifier and the glorified, Glory Himself, is truly hidden."

This conviction informed my mom as well. For she believed the Gospel changed everything.

Spending time with her during the last week of her life in hospice was both deeply sad and amazingly redemptive and beautiful. It was such a blessing to witness her saying goodbye to family and friends — as she reflected on her life, gave advice, and let the light of Christ shine forth from her as she faced death with no fear.

When I asked my children to reflect on a favorite memory of my mom, they reminisced about spending time in her home — including watching movies she selected for our evening entertainment. From To Kill a Mockingbird to Anne of Green Gables to an obscure black-and-white classic, we never knew what she'd planned for us to view together.

One of the most memorable films we enjoyed was Coat of Many Colors — the story of a young Dolly Parton and her family growing up in poverty in the Great Smoky Mountains of Tennessee. In fact, 13 million viewers watched the premiere on December 10, 2015 —prompting NBC to re-air the film on Christmas night that year we visited.

The film was powerful not only because it showed the real pain and trials of Dolly and her family, but also because it showed redemption and reconciliation.

Reflecting on Dolly's recent passing, I thought these themes, in many ways, captured my mom's heart and approach to life as a wife, mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and friend.

Growing up in humble surroundings, she too looked for redemptive elements in life — whether it was family, church, community, literature, art, film, or music

Along these lines, she kept an old Baptist Hymnal that she found at a garage sale with her Bible. As I was preparing for her eulogy, I found an inscription she wrote at the front: "There is great strength in these hymns. The words come to me even in my sleep. I love to wake up with a song already playing in my soul. The songs are planted in my heart through years of singing them."

Flipping through the hymnal, I discovered that she had hearted the song "I Need Thee Every Hour." I now understood why, in her final days in hospice, when she barely opened her eyes, she started singing with me when I read the song "Lord I Need You, Oh I need you, Every hour I need you" from the timely Worship Initiative devotional that aired that week.

It was a beautiful, powerful moment that demonstrated these songs sown in her spirit—and the hope and comfort they brought to her as she faced death. As a matter of fact, the last week in hospice showed me not only her deep love of the Lord, her family and friends, but also a heart for reconciliation.

As I read through Gone From My Sight: The Dying Experience that week — provided by many hospice facilities around the country to walk through this process — I learned how "unfinished business" can be a big factor "in determining how much resistance we put into meeting death."

Due to a challenging family situation, she had not seen two of her grandchildren since my father’s funeral eight years earlier. Nevertheless, when they heard about my mom’s condition, they arrived just in time to say their goodbyes. Knowing she had prayed to see them again and be reconciled, I was so thankful for the sweet time she had with both, leading her to tell my nephew that she could now die.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

It would be the last conversation she had before passing two days later.

In regard to my grandson’s question the afternoon of my mom’s funeral, the pastor responded beautifully, explaining that we would one day see her again — not in the feeble, frail state she had left the world — but as St. Paul described to the Church of Corinth, in her heavenly body. For "in Christ all shall be made alive…[and] raised in glory," (I Corinthians 15).

A great comfort as we ponder the weight of eternity.

item.title: Elon Musk's mom Maye nearly turned down SI Swimsuit cover over 'wrinkles and cellulite'
item.description: Maye Musk nearly turned down her Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover over wrinkle fears, but a phone call from her daughter changed everything.
item.content:encoded:
Maye Musk nearly passed on the chance to make a splash in Sports Illustrated Swimsuit because she worried about looking "wrinkly" in the iconic magazine.

The Canadian-born, South African-raised model made history in 2022 as the oldest Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover model at 74. Martha Stewart later broke the record at 81 in 2023. Now, Musk is looking back at the milestone and her journey from a single mother of three to a sought-after model in her new book, "Timeless."

"At my age, you have wrinkles and cellulite on your arms and on your thighs, so I prefer to wear long sleeves," the mother of tech mogul Elon Musk told Fox News Digital. "So, the idea of wearing a swimsuit was very uncomfortable. But then my daughter called me. I told her they were going to be shooting in Belize. She instantly said, 'You've got to go. Belize is beautiful.' So, I did. I took a chance."

MAYE MUSK DEFENDS SYDNEY SWEENEY'S NUDE SPORTS AD AND RECALLS 12-YEAR PATH TO CITIZENSHIP

In the book, Musk wrote, "I was still 73. My skin showed the signs of my weight having cycled up and down so many times in my life, including for each of my pregnancies. I'm wrinkly and I have cellulite. Swimsuit model?"

Despite her worries, Musk said she felt at ease when she began posing for photographer Yu Tsai. She even wore colorful two-pieces for the occasion.

"It was very unusual," she said with a laugh. "I've been told all of my life that I'm not a swimsuit model. When you think of swimsuit models, you think of the Victoria's Secret models. Those are really special body shapes. So it was a challenge for me. But as I say, you have to take a chance in life. And I knew they're not going to publish ugly photos. At one point, I felt so at ease that I even started dancing with the local people. I was in awe of exploring a new country, a new culture. That's what I love doing. And I got to celebrate me."

WATCH: MAYE MUSK DISCUSSES RAISING ELON MUSK, ESCAPING TOXIC MARRIAGE IN NEW MEMOIR ‘TIMELESS’

Looking back, Musk said she wonders why she was so nervous.

"When women go to the beach, they wrap a towel around themselves," she said. "But men, they could be obese, and they're still strutting in Speedos with such confidence. We really have to make a change. And if any man insults your body, well, they can get lost. There's always going to be somebody who feels the need to trash on you. It's not fair. But it's all about embracing who you are and not apologizing for that."

Musk didn't undergo a makeover to appear younger for the cover. Her signature silver hair remained untouched.

"Why do I need to color my hair?" Musk said. "You have to do the roots every four weeks, and I used to do them myself. Your hair then becomes very brittle because it's so damaged. And it grows out. And then I decided to cut my hair short. Soon after, I had four billboards in Times Square. I didn't feel like a granny. I felt fashionable."

It wasn't the first time Musk took a chance on a modeling gig.

In her book, Musk describes a phone call she received from her agent: "Tomorrow, you pose naked for the cover of TIME magazine. You're the only model they want and they won't budge." 

Musk had never done a nude shoot because, as she wrote, "nobody had ever asked."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Before stripping down, Musk sought advice from her children.

"I picked up the phone to dial Elon first, then stopped myself," Musk wrote. "I already knew what he would say: 'Absolutely not.' He was not the kind of son who wanted his mother naked on magazine covers. Not prudish, but definitely more conservative when it came to nudity. So I called Tosca. I wasn't too surprised to find that she was not in love with the idea, either. 'You never do naked!' she said. Her instinct was protective, not wanting me to risk an uncomfortable experience."

"Finally, I called Kimbal," she wrote. "Of my three children, he is the most relaxed and free-spirited. (He met his current wife at Burning Man.) He had a completely different perspective. ‘It’s TIME magazine. It’s journalism,’ he said. ‘Not some nudie magazine. It’ll be tasteful. You have nothing to worry about. Do it.’"

Musk told Fox News Digital it was important for her to get her children's approval before posing nude.

"Well, would you want your mother naked on the front cover of a magazine?" she said. 

"But it was Kimbal who encouraged me. He said it would be tasteful. He's always been a free spirit. And I trust him. When I arrived for the photoshoot, they were very careful with me. You have a makeup artist who has to go through your whole body. Then they did my hair and very plain makeup. Then they sat me with a mirror in front of me, so I could see exactly what the photographer sees."

"The photographer came in for the shoot, and maybe five minutes later, it was over," she said. "It was really quick and very respectful. They immediately brought a robe for me. I got changed and went home. That's all there was to it."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

For Musk, aging with confidence isn't just about embracing wrinkles and silver hair. The longtime dietitian also believes that taking care of your health plays an important role in feeling your best at any age.

"It gets harder to lose weight as you get older," Musk said. "With my patients, I always tell them to plan ahead. If you get hungry, there's no salad next to you. There's a donut. Also, only eat when you're hungry. And when you are hungry, make sure there is healthy food around, no desserts or chocolates. And if my patient didn't take the journey seriously, I would tell them, 'You can't come anymore.'"

"Even 10 pounds can make you feel uncomfortable," she said. "Everything is tight and you don't have confidence. You have to track your food intake. If a patient goes off what I recommended, they need to explain why. You need to hold yourself accountable if you want to make smarter choices for your health."

Musk said each decade of her life has been better than the last. At 78, she's happily embracing aging and hopes other women will do the same.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"When my mom was 86, she moved from South Africa to Canada and started all over," Musk said. "She was an artist. When she was nearing 90, her hands weren't strong enough to do the wood carvings she loved. So, by 94, she started doing computer art. My older sister taught her. She died at 98. But she always remained curious and busy. She was always exploring."

"You're never too old to start again," Musk said. "And don't worry about the wrinkles. A man doesn't care if he gets wrinkles. He still has his confidence. When you get insecure, you become less attractive. I didn't do anything to my face because I wanted to frown and have expression. But also, don't mix with people who make you feel insecure. They're not your friends. And there will be people who will push you down. You can't stay down. You just have to get up and show your talents, who you are."

item.title: Hollywood jobs flee overseas as Congress scrambles to stop production exodus — with Trump's blessing
item.description: A bipartisan bill aims to create a federal film tax credit to stop movie and TV production from fleeing overseas to Europe and Canada.
item.content:encoded:
Congress is scrambling to stop one of the United States' most iconic industries from fleeing overseas and taking thousands of jobs along with it.

The U.S. TV and film industry has been hemorrhaging work for years as production companies and movie studios flee to places like Europe and Canada for friendlier tax regimes and other attractive financial policies. It prompted President Donald Trump to publicly call on Congress to pass legislation aimed at incentivizing entertainment studios to bring their production back home — and an unlikely alliance of lawmakers is heeding the call.

A new bill that could potentially end up in a bipartisan tax package at the end of this year would push film and TV studios to bring their productions back to the U.S. via new tax incentives, with extra support if they choose to bring development to rural communities.

TRUMP CALLS HOLLYWOOD A 'TOTAL DISASTER,' PUSHES FEDERAL TAX INCENTIVE FOR FILM AFTER MEETING WITH JON VOIGHT

"Since I was a child, I was moved and inspired by the stories of America's greatness, by living out the American dream, and by the notion that I could do and achieve anything in this world, if I set my mind to it, and most of that was driven by a whole lot of American-made movies," Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I want this next generation to be inspired the same way, and I do not want American storytelling to go overseas, to be diluted by values from overseas."

Moran's East Texas congressional district is largely rural and a far cry from the Sunset Strip that was home to much of America's filmmaking history.

PELOSI, OMAR JOIN TRUMP AND SCHIFF AS UNLIKELY ALLIANCE PUSHES TO ONSHORE KEY INDUSTRY

He's one of the House lawmakers leading the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, a bill aimed at bringing film and TV jobs back to the U.S. by creating a federal tax credit for domestic productions. It would further incentivize studios to film in rural areas with added financial benefits in areas deemed to be federal opportunity zones.

"This bill is extremely important to send a message that American storytelling does not just happen in California or New York. It happens all over America, including rural America," Moran said.

The bill is notably led in the Senate by Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., a top Trump foe, and Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., one of the president's biggest supporters in the chamber.

Moran's House colleagues who are helping to spearhead the bill include Reps. Mike Carey, R-Ohio, Brian Jack, R-Ga., Linda Sanchez, D-Calif., and Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y.

'AMERICAN IDOL' DITCHES HOLLYWOOD FOR GEORGIA AFTER TWO DECADES AS CALIFORNIA LOSES ANOTHER PRODUCTION

Suozzi told Fox News Digital that his home state was "watching good-paying jobs and production move overseas," adding, "We can't let that happen."

"Democrats and Republicans agree we need to keep these jobs here," Suozzi said.

FILM PRODUCER SAYS 'MADE IN AMERICA' MOVIES CAN HELP REVIVE HOLLYWOOD'S STRUGGLING INDUSTRY

But some, particularly on the right, might bristle at the prospect of awarding more lenient tax policies to an industry they perceive as having a longtime liberal bias — something Moran pushed back on.

Moran said his state, for example, was home to "conservative," "faith-based," and "patriotic" entertainment production that was also creating jobs and stimulating local economies.

"So I would say to those that are challenging this, I would say, well, do you want to see the stories and the movies and the TV productions that we watch go overseas, and be influenced by the culture and the values of other countries, somewhere else that do not love freedom like we do in America?" he posed.

But the end of this congressional term is fast approaching, and getting anything passed after the November election will be an uphill battle.

"I feel confident that there will be some kind of bipartisan tax package during the lame-duck session, and my hope would be that this, or a version of this bill, makes it into the final text," Moran said.

item.title: WWE star CM Punk honors late New Found Glory founding member Chad Gilbert at Money in the Bank
item.description: CM Punk wore a "ChadBall" tribute on his white jacket entering the Smoothie King Center, honoring late New Found Glory founder Chad Gilbert.
item.content:encoded:
WWE star CM Punk entered the Smoothie King Center in New Orleans with hopes of climbing the ladder, grabbing the briefcase and earning a world title shot anywhere, any time.

But he appeared to be wrestling with a heavy heart.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

Punk was wearing a sharp white jacket with the "ChadBall" on the right side of his chest. WWE announcer Corey Graves pointed out that the phrase was in honor of the late New Found Glory founding member Chad Gilbert, who died at the age of 45 after a bout with adrenal cancer.

When Gilbert’s death was announced last month, Punk paid tribute to the guitarist in a post on Instagram. The photo showed Gilbert playing with Punk’s dog Larry, who also passed away earlier this year.

"This isn’t goodbye. I’ll see you tomorrow," he captioned the post.

Gilbert had battled adrenal cancer since 2021 and underwent brain surgery in February when doctors found tumors.

"On the morning of September 20th, Chad Everett Gilbert passed away peacefully in his sleep. He left this world surrounded by friends and family and took his final breaths with his wife and mother by his side, just as he wished," his family and the band wrote in a joint statement on social media on Sept. 20.

"We are devastated and shocked by how quickly he left us, yet so grateful for how peacefully and smoothly he went. The amount of visitors that crowded the hospital lobby at a moment’s notice is a testament to how beloved and cherished Chad was, and always will be. He was a legendary musician, but his favorite accomplishment was being a husband and father. His biggest dreams came true. He is survived by his wife, Lisa, his daughter, Lily, his mother, Jackie, and his brother, Brian."

Punk had kept Gilbert on his mind during several WWE shows over the years. He dedicated a victory at Bad Blood 2024 to the musician.

Fox News’ Ashley Hume contributed to this report.

item.title: WWE's Bron Breakker sends Je'Von Evans crashing through ambulance roof, Penta wins Money in the Bank match
item.description: Bron Breakker dominated with devastating spears, but a shocking Mexican Destroyer from Penta changed everything in the Money in the Bank ladder match.
item.content:encoded:
The Money in the Bank ladder match has a knack for providing must-see moments. It was no different on Saturday night as six men competed to grab the briefcase and earn a world title opportunity at any time.

Bron Breakker, Je’Von Evans, Penta, CM Punk, Kevin Owens and Trick Williams each gave it their all to win and possibly start a journey to holding gold. If there were live odds on the match, Breakker might have been at -30,000 because of his performance.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

Breakker delivered a devastating spear to Evans, leveling him into the barricade. WWE officials crowded around Evans as it appeared the "Young OG" was seriously injured. He was placed on a stretcher, carried to the back and placed into an ambulance. It appeared Evans’ night was over before it could even really begin.

The "Unpredictable Bad A—" had momentum on his side. He would tactically take out his opponents one by one, starting with Trick Williams and Penta. As Punk and Owens focused on each other as they have been for weeks on "SmackDown," they took their attention away from Breakker.

He targeted Punk and Owens next. He ran as hard as he could and speared both competitors through the barricade near the announce table. As he tried to get back to his feet, an ambulance began to drive down the entrance ramp.

Evans was back!

Evans took out Breakker and took care of his other opponents. It looked like Evans was about to make history as the youngest men’s Money in the Bank winner in history. However, he struggled to set up a 15-foot ladder to get his hands on the briefcase. Breakker was back in the ring and distracted the highflyer.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The two jockeyed for position and jostled the ladder out of position. Evans would have one last gasp but was way too far out to try to grab the briefcase. Breakker pushed the ladder, knocking Evans off it. Evans flew through the air and crashed through the roof of the ambulance.

It was the biggest WTF moment of the match.

Breakker thought he was in the clear, but Penta came back into the fray. The Luchador turned up the heat on Breakker. He wedged a small ladder in between the turnbuckle. As he and Breakker fought toward the top of it, Penta hit a nasty Mexican Destroyer on Breakker, catapulting him to the ground.

Penta climbed the ladder and won the Money in the Bank ladder match for the first time in his career.

Penta can now target Roman Reigns or Sami Zayn for their world titles.

item.title: Liv Morgan steals Women's World Championship at Money in the Bank, becomes 4-time winner
item.description: Liv Morgan stunned Stephanie Vaquer with Oblivion to capture the Women's World Championship for the fourth time in a chaotic triple-threat match.
item.content:encoded:
Triple-threat matches are always a scramble. You can throw alliances out the window. No one was about to help Stephanie Vaquer retain the Women’s World Championship and no one was going to help Becky Lynch or Liv Morgan put gold back around their waists.

Those words were evident throughout the match. Even as it seemed as though Vaquer and Lynch did their best to keep Morgan at bay and essentially make the match one-on-one, the two WWE superstars immediately cast that aside and went blow-for-blow throughout the match. Vaquer and Lynch couldn’t even agree on where to set up a table to possibly take Morgan out for good.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

Vaquer used her incredible ring prowess to stay on top throughout the match. She hit Lynch and Morgan with meteoras into the steel steps. Vaquer hit her corkscrew moonsault on Morgan and thought she had the win. But Lynch, using her savviness, pulled the referee out of the ring before she could count to three.

Each fighter went all out. Vaquer kicked Lynch, who was on top of the apron. Lynch fell backward but didn’t go through the table. Instead, the table’s legs snapped. While Vaquer’s attention was turned to "The Man," Morgan appeared out of nowhere and hit Vaquer with Oblivion.

She pinned Vaquer to pick up the win.

Vaquer was emotional as she watched Morgan celebrate. Lynch was on the outside trying to gather herself after the vicious table slam.

Morgan has cast herself as the "greatest women’s champion of alllllllllllllllllllllll time." She’s certainly close to proving that in terms of the reigns she has had. Morgan has won the Women’s World Championship twice in this calendar year alone, pinning Vaquer both times for the title in 2026.

It’s the fourth time Morgan has held the title. The Judgment Day might be on a downturn, but Morgan continues to be a shining light in the faction. Moreover, she didn’t need anyone to come and help her either.

item.title: Abbas delays Palestinian elections again, making more than two decades without vote
item.description: Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas delayed elections to 2027, extending a nearly 20-year wait as Israel and Hamas clash over the blame.
item.content:encoded:
More than two decades after being elected to what was supposed to be a four-year term, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has once again postponed elections, extending a nearly 20-year wait for voters to choose a new legislature.

Abbas issued a decree Friday pushing Palestinian Legislative Council elections from next month to Sept. 11, 2027, according to the official Palestinian news agency WAFA. Presidential elections, which have not been held since Abbas' 2005 victory, are also scheduled for that date.

The delay allows Palestinian leaders to remain in power without facing voters and could further damage the credibility of the Palestinian Authority, which has faced criticism over corruption and its security cooperation with Israel.

NICARAGUA'S ORTEGA SAYS COUNTRY WILL 'NEVER AGAIN' HOLD ELECTIONS, SHUTTING OUT OPPOSITION

The Palestinian Authority, dominated by Abbas' Fatah party, governs parts of the West Bank under agreements reached in the 1990s.

Palestinian officials cited conditions in the West Bank, Gaza Strip and east Jerusalem as reasons for postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, claimed Israel had blocked election materials and international observers from entering Gaza, according to The Associated Press.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar rejected the claim, accusing Abbas of trying to shift blame for the delay.

Abbas' "attempt to drag Israel into this, falsely claiming that Israel imposed obstacles to holding elections, is yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability," Saar wrote on X.

Hamas, meanwhile, welcomed the postponement, calling it "a step in the right direction" and urging further talks on rebuilding Palestinian institutions before holding elections.

Palestinians last held legislative elections in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries subsequently boycotted the Hamas-led government, fueling unrest that ended with Hamas taking control of Gaza in 2007.

IRAN REAFFIRMS SUPPORT FOR HAMAS AS TRUMP PUSHES TO DISARM TERROR GROUP

Since then, Hamas has controlled Gaza while Abbas' Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority has governed parts of the West Bank.

The postponed election also threatened to bring new challenges to Abbas' leadership. Before the delay, Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and a faction led by Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah security chief who fell out with Abbas, had been discussing an unlikely political alliance.

"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.

The decision comes as the Palestinian Authority's future role in Gaza remains uncertain under a U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year.

The plan calls for the authority to eventually play a role in Gaza, but its immediate responsibilities remain unclear. Hamas continues to govern the territory, while a committee of Palestinian technocrats remains in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza and oversee a transition of power.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Packers get revenge chance as Bears lean on run game without Caleb Williams
item.description: The Bears are 3-point favorites, but Caleb Williams remains sidelined and Tyson Bagent must lead Chicago's run-heavy attack into Green Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Rivalries add fuel to the flame in multiple games each year. You get matchups that just stand out because of the history of the teams. The fans get a bit more excited, there is more news coverage, and, in general, the games seem to be better. This week we get the Bears and Packers squaring off – one of the biggest rivalries in all the NFL.

The Bears are -3 point favorites at the Packers. If Caleb Williams were playing in the game, I could potentially understand it. However, he is still out for this game. The Bears believe in Tyson Bagent, but I’m not as much of a believer. Chicago wants to run the ball as much as possible and control the clock. That’s how they’ve won the past two games without Williams.

The Packers have one of the worst rush defenses in the league. That does mean the Bears should have a major advantage. It isn’t just one running back that Chicago is leaning on, either. item.title: Abdul El-Sayed feuds with Dave Portnoy over response to Michigan cheating allegation comments
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed mocked Dave Portnoy's athleticism after Portnoy called the Michigan Senate nominee a "terrorist" over a Wolverines cheating joke.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed mocked Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy on Saturday, commenting on Portnoy's body and athleticism.

El-Sayed's comment came after Portnoy called the Democrat a "terrorist" over a joke about the Wolverines cheating.

"Meanwhile, here’s [Portnoy] committing an act of athletic terrorism. Less pizza, more gym, habibi," El-Sayed wrote on X over a clip of Portnoy sprinting on a turf field.

EL-SAYED QUESTIONS ETHICS OF FOOTBALL IN RESURFACED AUDIO

The exchange followed a clip of El-Sayed, a University of Michigan graduate, joking about his alma mater’s football program.

"Is Michigan going to win a game without cheating? I say this as a Wolverine," El-Sayed said in a clip.

Portnoy responded, "This guy really is a terrorist." El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, shared Portnoy’s post and wrote that Portnoy "is exactly right."

Asked whether Rogers actually believed El-Sayed was a terrorist, Rogers spokeswoman Alyssa Brouillet told The Detroit News, "Parroting Ohio State talking points is a bridge too far."

El-Sayed’s football jab followed Michigan’s sign-stealing scandal.

In August 2025, the NCAA announced multimillion-dollar financial penalties, recruiting restrictions and four additional years of probation after finding an impermissible scouting scheme involving former staffer Connor Stalions.

In 2024, its football program acknowledged impermissible recruiting contacts during the COVID-19 recruiting dead period, improper tryouts and unauthorized coaching by noncoaching staff. The NCAA separately found that former coach Jim Harbaugh provided false or misleading information to investigators.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Under former coach Rich Rodriguez, Michigan received three years of probation in 2010 and a 130-hour reduction in practice time after violations involving excessive practice and training activities. The school’s basketball program also faced sanctions over improper loans from booster Ed Martin to four players, including Chris Webber, resulting in forfeited victories, scholarship reductions and four years of probation.

The social media clash also comes as El-Sayed faces criticism over his responses to questions about Iran’s regime and Islamist organizations.

At a September town hall, Iranian-American student Iman Dashti described his family’s alleged mistreatment by Iranian authorities and pressed El-Sayed to condemn the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Islamic Republic. El-Sayed responded by opposing American-led regime change and arguing that Iran’s people should determine their government, drawing criticism for avoiding a direct condemnation.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

During an Oct. 5 interview, Fox News host Martha MacCallum repeatedly asked whether he supported terrorist designations for Muslim Brotherhood organizations in Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon. El-Sayed answered that he would support designating organizations engaged in political violence, without explicitly naming the Brotherhood in his responses.

Rogers renewed criticism of El-Sayed’s responses concerning terrorist groups during their Oct. 8 debate. El-Sayed also declined to identify Iran or Israel as the greater threat to the United States, saying both had proven dangerous in their own way.

El-Sayed has, however, publicly condemned Hamas. During an August appearance on "The Jim Acosta Show," he said, "I think they’re wrong. I think they committed war crimes," while also accusing Israel of war crimes and genocide.

El-Sayed has also criticized football’s culture, writing in an October 2021 essay that "toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport" ran deeper than the emails that prompted then-Raiders coach Jon Gruden’s resignation.

Responding to Gruden’s racist, homophobic and misogynistic messages, El-Sayed recalled experiencing racist taunting in football locker rooms and argued that coaches needed to address the culture behind such behavior.

item.title: WNBA Finals: Angel Reese headlines championship showdown as league seeks to draw viewers without Caitlin Clark
item.description: With Caitlin Clark and the Fever eliminated, Angel Reese's Atlanta Dream face the Golden State Valkyries in a huge WNBA Finals viewership test.
item.content:encoded:
The WNBA didn't get Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham in the Finals, but it may have gotten the next best thing in terms of viewership hopes.

Angel Reese’s Atlanta Dream face the Golden State Valkyries in a best-of-seven series beginning Oct. 17, matching a franchise seeking its first championship against an expansion team chasing a title in its second season.

Both organizations also bring distinctive cultural identities. Atlanta’s players once campaigned against their own Republican co-owner, supporting Democrat Raphael Warnock. Golden State has embraced LGBTQ outreach through Pride celebrations, drag performances and community partnerships.

Those histories offer another layer to a matchup with straightforward basketball questions: Can Golden State prevent Reese from creating second chances, and can Atlanta’s defense generate enough easy baskets to win the championship?

CAITLIN CLARK'S LOWEST-RATED PLAYOFF GAME STILL OUTDREW EVERY NON-FEVER FIRST-ROUND BROADCAST

These Finals could provide an indication of the WNBA’s current drawing power without Clark, and just how much star power Angel Reese has.

Reese brings a substantial following of her own. Her Instagram account had approximately 5.3 million followers as of Oct. 10, which is the most of any WNBA player and more than one million more than Clark.

Her visibility extends beyond basketball. She has a signature Reebok shoe and became the first female athlete featured in a national McDonald’s meal collaboration in 2025. Those partnerships have put her name before consumers who may not regularly watch the WNBA.

Her first Finals appearance now offers an opportunity to see whether that recognition translates into viewers following her pursuit of a championship, with Clark and the Fever eliminated.

There are substantial audiences to measure against. Indiana’s decisive first-round loss to Las Vegas averaged 2.25 million viewers across USA Network and CNBC. Atlanta’s semifinal opener against New York averaged 1.2 million on ABC, according to Sports Media Watch. The games aired on different networks and in different time slots, making them benchmarks rather than a direct measure of either player’s individual appeal.

The league has already demonstrated that a Finals without either Clark or Reese can attract a sizable audience. Last year’s Las Vegas–Phoenix championship series averaged 1.5 million viewers across ABC and ESPN, the second-most-watched Finals on ESPN networks behind 2024.

This year’s series will air across NBC, USA Network and Peacock, adding another consideration to comparisons with previous championships.

One series cannot establish the league’s permanent audience ceiling. But Reese’s championship debut could help show how much of her substantial off-court following—and the broader interest surrounding the WNBA—will follow her onto its biggest stage.

Atlanta brings a history of campaigning against a Republican co-owner, while Golden State has established prominent ties to LGBTQ advocacy.

The Dream’s political activism drew national attention in 2020, when then-co-owner Republican Sen. Kelly Loeffler opposed the WNBA’s embrace of the Black Lives Matter movement. She urged the league to replace planned Black Lives Matter and "Say Her Name" warmup apparel with American flags.

"The truth is, we need less — not more politics in sports," Loeffler wrote to then-Commissioner Cathy Engelbert.

Dream players and others across the league responded by wearing "Vote Warnock" shirts, supporting Democrat Raphael Warnock in his challenge to Loeffler. Atlanta’s Elizabeth Williams described the effort as voluntary and driven by players. Warnock defeated Loeffler in the January 2021 runoff.

AMERICANS CLASH OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES AS DEBATE HEATS UP: ‘JUST GETTING OUTRAGEOUS'

The following month, the league approved the Dream’s sale to an ownership group comprising Larry Gottesdiener, Suzanne Abair and former Dream guard Renee Montgomery. Montgomery, who had sat out the 2020 season to focus on social justice work, remains a co-owner and vice president. The franchise’s official biography highlights her advocacy for social justice and equality in women’s sports. Those events preceded Reese’s arrival in Atlanta by several years.

Golden State, which began playing in 2025, has a shorter organizational history but has made LGBTQ outreach a visible part of its identity.

Its second annual Pride Game, against Atlanta on June 26, featured a surrounding celebration with drag performances, Pride merchandise and a halftime lineup featuring Sasha Colby. The franchise also announced participation in four regional Pride celebrations and sponsorship of the San Francisco International LGBTQ+ Film Festival.

The Valkyries’ advocacy earned recognition from Equality California and the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, along with a Community Ally Award from the Harvey Milk LGBTQ Democratic Club.

After Golden State’s victory over Atlanta that Pride Night, Gabby Williams celebrated toward a camera with the declaration, "For the gays!"

Williams and Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase have also publicly supported transgender athletes participating in women’s sports.

Before an Aug. 2 game, Nakase said her emphasis on inclusion extended to transgender women.

"I’m all about women, little girls deserving to play, and that includes trans women," she said.

Williams expressed a similar position during a May 19 media scrum, before clip resurfaced and spread widely in August.

"I would welcome a trans athlete on my team or against my team, anytime," Williams told reporters.

Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom subsequently cited Williams’ support as an inspiration for his announced bid to enter the 2027 WNBA draft.

During an Aug. 14 interview with former Auburn coach Bruce Pearl, Freedom recalled seeing comments welcoming transgender teammates and opponents and deciding to pursue the opportunity himself. Freedom later confirmed to OutKick that it was Williams' comments that inspired him.

"If they don’t have any problem with it, why not just go out there and take my shot?" Freedom said.

This championship series will also close a chapter for the WNBA’s leadership. Commissioner Cathy Engelbert announced in September that she will retire at the end of 2026, making Atlanta’s matchup with Golden State the last Finals of her tenure.

Her final season began with uncertainty over whether labor negotiations would disrupt the league’s schedule. The eventual agreement delivered substantial raises for players and a seven-year deal running through 2032, giving her successor a foundation for the years ahead.

Questions about officiating and player safety continued during the season. In June, Phoenix’s Alyssa Thomas received a one-game suspension after making contact with her fist to Clark’s throat. Officials did not call a foul during the play; the league imposed the punishment after reviewing it. Indiana coach Stephanie White publicly criticized the officiating afterward.

Away from the court, league officials and players also confronted online harassment and a widening debate over transgender athletes in women’s sports. An August meeting of the league’s anti-hate task force addressed both subjects. The WNBA said there were no immediate eligibility matters affecting the league and pledged further discussions with teams and the players’ association.

Some changes will arrive after Engelbert leaves. A centralized replay center is scheduled to launch in 2027, giving officials access to additional camera angles and assistance reviewing eligible plays. Its introduction will provide an early opportunity for the next commissioner to demonstrate progress on a recurring source of frustration.

Expansion will also continue, with Cleveland beginning play in 2028, Detroit in 2029 and Philadelphia in 2030. That means more markets, more roster spots and more pressure to turn growing interest into sustained support.

Against that backdrop, these Finals offer a look at the league Engelbert is leaving behind—and the task ahead: building lasting audiences for more teams and players while addressing the disputes that have accompanied the WNBA’s growth.

And there will be some actual basketball being played too.

Reese reached her first WNBA Finals after averaging 16.4 points and 12.1 rebounds during the regular season and winning Defensive Player of the Year.

Golden State’s Kiah Stokes could make those opportunities harder to find. She helped defend A’ja Wilson during the semifinals and collected 14 rebounds in the opener. The battle near the basket will test whether Reese can establish position and create second chances against another experienced rebounder.

At the other end, Gabby Williams has taken on a larger scoring role for Golden State. She enters the Finals averaging about 23 points in the playoffs, up from roughly 14 during the regular season. Atlanta must decide how much defensive attention to give her without leaving other Valkyries open.

Williams has already shown she will trust those teammates. Late in the second semifinal game against Las Vegas, she passed to Veronica Burton, whose only basket of the night was a decisive 3-pointer. Tiffany Hayes added 21 points off the bench, demonstrating how Golden State can find scoring help beyond its starters.

Atlanta has its own player capable of controlling a game without dominating the headlines. Jordin Canada scored 19 points and set up 11 baskets for teammates in the win that clinched the Dream’s Finals berth. Her ability to find Howard and Reese—or attack the basket herself—will be important against Golden State’s league-leading defense.

Golden State won all three regular-season meetings with Atlanta. The Dream now bring additional playoff experience through DeWanna Bonner, who arrived late in the season, while Allisha Gray’s recovery from a hand injury remains a major consideration.

The central contest is straightforward: Atlanta needs Canada to create good opportunities and Reese to keep possessions alive. Golden State needs Williams to continue leading its offense while Stokes and her teammates prevent the Dream from getting repeated chances at the basket.

item.title: Hunters say harvesting their own food deepens important connection to God
item.description: Chad and James Hampton spend hours in a Michigan tree stand each hunting season, filling freezers with venison as an expression of Christian faith.
item.content:encoded:
For twin brothers Chad and James Hampton, putting food on the table can begin hours earlier — sitting quietly in a Michigan tree stand.

The pastors, authors and avid outdoorsmen harvest several deer during hunting season each year, filling their freezers with venison to be eaten.

But to the brothers, harvesting their own food represents more than providing meals for their families. It's also intertwined with their Christian faith.

'MEATEATER' HOST SAYS WILD GAME IS 'THE HEALTHIEST FOOD' AMERICANS CAN EAT

"We know that God's given us that food to manage and also consume so that we can be what He's created us to be," Chad Hampton told Fox News Digital.

The Hamptons, founders of Huntin' the Truth Ministries and hosts of the outdoor show "Twin Factor," point to Genesis 1:26 when explaining their view of hunters as stewards of God's creation.

"We're managing God's creation that He gave to us," Chad Hampton said.

The connection between faith, food and the outdoors also appears in their new book, "100 Days of Strength for Hunters," a devotional designed to help outdoorsmen strengthen their relationship with God.

COWBOY CHEF SAYS AMERICANS ARE TURNING TO ONE OF THE 'HEALTHIEST MEATS,' AND IT'S AT MOST GROCERY STORES

The brothers said the book combines Scripture, hunting stories, practical applications and prayer — and is short enough for hunters to take with them into the tree stand.

Their approach to food also overlaps with a larger national conversation about eating "real food" and knowing where food comes from, themes that have been promoted by the Make America Healthy Again movement.

It's a message that resonates with the Hamptons.

"Everything that we harvest we eat," James Hampton said.

They also believe many Americans have become disconnected from their food as convenience increasingly shapes what people eat.

The Hamptons readily acknowledge they aren't immune to eating fast food, pointing to their busy schedules.

"Although we love our fast food, we also love the slow-cooked venison," Chad Hampton said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Hunting, however, requires something convenience cannot provide — time.

The brothers said they could spend hours in a tree stand pursuing an animal they would ultimately bring home and eat. That process, they believe, carries a responsibility rooted in their faith.

They view it as both harvesting food and caring for what they believe God has entrusted to them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

That same relationship between hunting and Christianity has guided their ministry for more than two decades.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

James Hampton recalled praying from a tree stand during a difficult period in 2004, while his wife was battling cancer. The experience ultimately helped inspire the brothers' ministry and its mission of teaching others to "hunt for God and His plan for their life."

"We have to live what we preach," James Hampton said. "And that is loving God with all our hearts, souls, minds and strengths and seeking Him."

item.title: Real-life exorcist reveals eerie encounter, warns Hollywood misses most terrifying part of demonic possession
item.description: Father Carlos Martins reveals what Hollywood gets wrong about demonic possession and why the devil's mind is more terrifying than any spectacle.
item.content:encoded:
Hollywood has spent decades frightening audiences with spinning heads, levitating bodies and priests shouting down demons. But Catholic exorcist Father Carlos Martins says the most terrifying part of alleged demonic possession isn't what the audience can see. It's what they can't.

"The thing that Hollywood doesn't pick up well is the demonic mind," Fr. Martins told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview ahead of Halloween, as the third season of "The Exorcist Files" podcast gets underway.

"It picks up [the devil's] demonic power well, throwing of chairs, the screaming, levitating and so on and so forth. But his rage, his inner anger, his disgust with humans and God, that it doesn't get well."

FATHER CARLOS MARTINS RECOUNTS CHILLING EXORCISM, CLAIMS WOMAN MOVED OBJECTS WITHOUT TOUCHING THEM

Fr. Martins, who co-hosts the podcast with co-creator Ryan Bethea, described what he believes Hollywood misses about the psychological dimension of alleged demonic encounters, including an incident in which he said a person undergoing an exorcism threatened to bomb a flight he was scheduled to take the following day.

"Why are you here? You're not supposed to be here. I'm going to bomb your flight tomorrow," Fr. Martins recalled hearing while assisting another exorcist.

The priest said he subsequently changed his flight, not because of the threat, but because the session had been so productive that he offered to remain for additional appointments.

When he returned the next day, Fr. Martins said, the person appeared surprised by his presence.

CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

"You weren't supposed to be here," he recalled the possessed person saying.

Fr. Martins interpreted the encounter as evidence of what he believes is the extraordinary but imperfect intelligence of the devil and demonic beings. He said the apparent knowledge of his original flight contrasted with the alleged demonic entity's failure to anticipate his changed plans.

For Fr. Martins, the encounter was a chilling example of why he believes the most frightening aspect of demonic possession has very little to do with the supernatural spectacles audiences see on-screen.

The third season of "The Exorcist Files" launched Oct. 5, with new episodes scheduled to roll out over the next two months.

Among the new cases is an especially complicated account involving multiple family members, according Bethea.

IOWA CITY COUNCIL MEETING ERUPTS AFTER FORMER MEMBER OPENS WITH SATANIC PRAYER AND 'HAIL SATAN'

"There is one particular episode this season that involves so many moving parts and multiple family members being demonized," Bethea told Fox News Digital.

The case, he added, "actually spans hundreds of years."

Bethea said the story may encourage listeners to examine unresolved trauma, mental health concerns and other personal struggles that he and Fr. Martins believe may contribute to spiritual vulnerability.

The podcast, which dramatizes purported exorcism case files, has also challenged Bethea's own understanding of spiritual warfare.

After working with Fr. Martins and hearing similar accounts from other exorcists, Bethea said he has become more confident in his Christian faith rather than more fearful of the supernatural.

"I have walked away feeling, ironically, less scared and more confident than ever," he said.

SACRED PAGES OF 1,000-YEAR-OLD GOSPEL REVEAL ANCIENT DNA SCIENTISTS NEVER EXPECTED

Fr. Martins warned that what he considers the greatest danger of demonic influence is not necessarily its physical manifestations, but the intimate knowledge he believes the devil and evil forces possess about their targets.

"When you're dealing with the devil, you're dealing with an entity that has observed you your whole life," Fr. Martins said. "He knows your weaknesses. He knows where your soft spots are. He knows what your preferences are."

"So he knows exactly where to press and how hard to cause maximal damage," the priest added.

Fr. Martins cautioned against attempting to confront demonic forces without spiritual preparation, arguing that human intelligence alone is no match for the adversary he describes as the "ancient serpent."

The priest acknowledged that the 1973 horror classic "The Exorcist" remains, in his view, a compelling depiction of what can occur during an exorcism, although he singled out the film's famous head-spinning sequence as physically impossible.

He also described witnessing what appeared to be a person's canine teeth growing several inches, an experience he attributed to a supernatural illusion rather than an actual physical transformation.

POPE LEO VISITS SITE OF MIRACLE CURES, MEETS PEOPLE WHOSE UNEXPLAINED HEALINGS STUNNED DOCTORS

For Fr. Martins, however, the disturbing imagery is secondary to what he described as the hatred and irrationality of the demonic mind.

"Because that is the part of him that has no rational explanation," he said.

Despite the dramatic subject matter, Fr. Martins said the actual practice of exorcism is considerably less theatrical than its Hollywood portrayal.

"I never yell at the devil. I've never heard of an exorcist doing that," Fr. Martins said.

He described exorcism as a generally calm process centered on prayer, spiritual reconciliation and helping the individual receiving assistance.

"The job of the exorcist is not to cast out the devil," Fr. Martins said.

Rather than attempting to overpower an alleged demon through increasingly forceful prayers, Fr. Martins said he seeks to understand why he believes the entity has gained influence over an individual and how that person can return to a state of reconciliation with Christ.

The priest also described exorcist training as largely an apprenticeship process, with less experienced priests learning alongside seasoned practitioners before conducting sessions independently.

FORMER TV ANCHOR WHO PLEADED GUILTY TO KILLING MOTHER LAST HALLOWEEN GETS LIFE SENTENCE

With Halloween approaching, Fr. Martins and Bethea also addressed whether ordinary holiday traditions pose spiritual dangers.

Fr. Martins said he does not oppose children dressing up or going trick-or-treating, although he would discourage costumes celebrating evil or demonic imagery.

"Would I allow my children to go trick or treating? Yeah, I would," Fr. Martins said. "I would never let them go dressed as something sordid. As something evil, as something devilish or demonic."

The priest said he would have no objection to children dressing as ordinary characters or participating in family-friendly Halloween traditions, provided the costumes did not celebrate something he considers contrary to his religious beliefs.

Bethea similarly defended activities such as trick-or-treating and harvest festivals, recalling how his mother enthusiastically created Halloween costumes when he was a child.

However, he cautioned against practices he associates with occult involvement.

MASSIVE 2,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY FROM TIME OF JESUS EMERGES REMARKABLY INTACT

The podcast has featured several cases involving Ouija boards, including an account in which a grandmother reportedly gave her grandson a board so they could communicate after her death.

Another case involved three children experimenting with a Ouija board, with one allegedly experiencing disturbing consequences, despite not having initiated the activity, according to Bethea.

He also identified astrology and tarot cards among practices the hosts discourage, arguing that they can expose people to what he believes are spiritual dangers.

"We would say there are plenty of fun, other games that you can play," Bethea said.

He jokingly suggested Risk and Monopoly as alternatives, before noting that greed could also be considered a sin.

Bethea emphasized that the show's accounts should not be interpreted as a reason to assume every unexplained experience has a supernatural cause, and pointed to psychological assessments and other scrutiny involved in determining whether someone should receive an exorcism.

The co-host also acknowledged that he had not seen evidence establishing Halloween as a universally heightened period of supernatural activity, despite hearing such claims from people interviewed for the podcast.

For both hosts, the larger message of "The Exorcist Files" is intended to be one of hope over fear.

Bethea said producing the series has strengthened his Christian faith, and listeners have contacted the show describing renewed religious commitment after hearing its stories.

Fr. Martins likewise said that although his work involves confronting what he believes to be demonic forces, he does not spend his personal life preoccupied with the devil.

"You know, the devil has a plan for you. But the good news is, so does God," he said. "Am I afraid of the devil? No, I'm afraid of being separated from Jesus Christ."

item.title: ‘Big Balls’ of DOGE fame gives exclusive look at new Trump mission to overhaul government
item.description: Edward Coristine reveals plans to make passport applications fully digital through America.gov, the AI-powered platform replacing thousands of sites.
item.content:encoded:
Edward Coristine, the former DOGE engineer better known as "Big Balls," is now helping build the Trump administration’s new digital front door to the federal government — an effort aimed at giving Americans one place to navigate information and, eventually, complete services now spread across thousands of government websites.

"I think that the fact that there’s 29,000 government websites is pretty insane," Coristine told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview. "And it is the citizens’ objective to have to go figure out which government website they’re supposed to use for each specific thing."

Coristine — better known around Washington by his attention-grabbing "Big Balls" nickname — sat down with Fox News Digital at the White House to talk about his new role helping build America.gov, what he learned during his time at DOGE, the administration’s plans to make more government services fully digital, his experience being attacked in Washington, and how the nickname that helped make him famous actually came from his dad.

TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE

Coristine is now working with the National Design Studio on the administration’s revamped America.gov, which launched Sept. 29 as an AI-powered single point of entry for information drawn from thousands of government websites. President Donald Trump singled out Coristine during the launch, identifying him as the project’s lead engineer and thanking him for his work.

Coristine said his time at DOGE gave him a firsthand look at the frustration Americans face when trying to navigate federal services and helped shape what he is working on now.

"I think we got a lot of feedback that the American government is hard to interact with because you have to navigate the maze of bureaucratic services," Coristine said.

The software engineer had already worked in Musk’s orbit before joining DOGE, spending several months at Neuralink, Musk’s brain-computer interface company, before later joining the government efficiency effort at 19.

"What I think is really special about America.gov is it presents a single point of entry to find all the information that you need," he added, including finding government services tailored to the user and asking questions with answers sourced from the federal government.

TRUMP TO USHER IN ‘GOLDEN AGE’ OF AMERICAN TECH WITH DC BASH SHOWCASING POWERFUL NEW TOOL

Coristine pointed to Medicare as one example, saying Americans currently may have to move between Medicare.gov and the Social Security website to enroll in benefits.

"Companies, generally speaking, only have one website and everything is easy to find," he said. "We should have the same vision for the government."

The ambitions for America.gov also go beyond simply helping users find the right information. Coristine said the administration plans to make first-time passport applications fully digital, expanding beyond the online renewal system already available to eligible Americans.

item.title: MARC SIEGEL: Russia's mysterious lab death exposes a danger the world isn't ready for
item.description: A Russian lab worker's mysterious pneumonia death raises urgent questions about plague, bioengineering and the lack of global health surveillance.
item.content:encoded:
Plague is an ancient scourge, and fear of the plague is buried deep in our unconscious. The Black Death caused over 100 million deaths in the 14th century, six centuries before the advent of antibiotics. Compare that to 50 to 100 million deaths from the Spanish flu in 1918 or over 15 million deaths from COVID. On top of severe illness and death, these devastating pandemics have caused worldwide fear and panic.

Flash forward six years from the origins of COVID, and once again we learn of a mysterious pneumonia death of a scientist, this time a laboratory worker, Darya Shipilova, who was working in a lab in Siberia that has been studying dangerous pathogens, including the plague.

Once again, as with COVID, there are far more questions than answers. Is the pathogen pneumonic plague? The Russians deny it. Has it been bioengineered to make it more resistant to antibiotics and more easily transmissible through the air? The Russian health authorities deny it. Have hundreds of patients been isolated and several hospitals been shut down out of an abundance of caution, as the health authorities there would have you believe, or is this something far worse, as it was during the initial Wuhan lockdown for COVID? Russia is now saying that it is winding down precautionary measures, but why were these extensive measures necessary in the first place?

MYSTERY DEATH AT RUSSIAN PLAGUE LAB TRIGGERS SWEEPING PRECAUTIONS AS US WATCHES CLOSELY

We may never have the answers to any of these questions, but unfortunately, they not only bring back bad memories of COVID, but they also unmask a continuing lack of a comprehensive global health surveillance network to protect us. The assertions and gesticulations by WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus at press conferences are no more reassuring now than they were back then.

US, WHO REQUEST DETAILS FROM RUSSIA AMID REPORTS OF SECOND PNEUMONIA CASE

The treatment for these scourges, both ancient and modern, for both fear and the actual disease, as I write in my new book, "The Angels Among Us," is messengers from God to reassure us, treat us, and guide us through, just as Dr. Stephen Kornfeld recently did on the hantavirus ship, the MV Hondius, when another scary disease, the Andes strain of hantavirus, emerged.

In fact, fear of an unknown pathogen sparking a global pandemic was the motivation for an international call for a global network of scientists to protect us more than two decades ago. Unfortunately, that so-called network failed miserably with COVID, as China’s smokescreen was famously amplified by the WHO’s declaration in January 2020 that this was only a regional problem. 

COVID whistleblower ophthalmologist Li Wenliang, who died in a Wuhan hospital from COVID in February 2020 after a middle-of-the-night visit from the police to shut him down, is buried deep in the public consciousness. So, too, are all our friends and patients who died unceremoniously in the first several months of the pandemic.

CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

One who didn’t die, as described in "The Angels Among Us," was Evie Rodriguez, who was saved not by medicines but by prayer. She was in the ICU at UC Davis, not responding to steroids or a new antiviral treatment (remdesivir), but rather than be overcome by fear, she turned to prayer and was visited by angels sent to her by her father, Pastor Sam Rodriguez. 

This gave her the strength she needed to fight off the angel of death. "I am fully awake, and a dark spirit with an open mouth comes into the room, and I can feel that it has come for me. To take me. It is very heavy and real, a dark force. I feel it is the spirit of death. I am not afraid. I become angry and demand it to leave. ‘What are you doing here?’ I yell. ‘Get away!’ And it goes away. I will it away."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The difference between 2020 and 2026 may be that the pathogen now, if it is plague, is potentially not very contagious, antibiotics can treat it, and there is already a vaccine that can be used against it, presuming it hasn’t been altered. So the risk beyond that initial case would appear to be very, very small.

But the fear and the global vulnerability remain. Laboratory accidents occur all the time. And we are not prepared for them, especially when it comes to dangerous pathogens from dangerous places. And there is an even more powerful pathogen spreading through our population than disease — fear.

item.title: NYPD detective gives update on condition after illegal immigrant duo allegedly stabbed him 7 times
item.description: Video shows Det. Jose Mercedes covered in blood after two suspects on an e-bike allegedly stabbed him seven times during a Bronx gold chain robbery.
item.content:encoded:
An NYPD detective who was stabbed and slashed seven times during a brazen Bronx robbery has been released from the hospital and is recovering from his injuries.

"I’m feeling much better, thank you," Det. Jose Mercedes, a 10-year NYPD veteran assigned to the 44th Precinct, told the New York Post on Saturday.

Mercedes, 33, was off duty Oct. 2 and cleaning out the trunk of his car in when two suspects allegedly ambushed him and tried to steal his gold chain, according to the NYPD.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECTS WITH LENGTHY CRIMINAL RECORDS ARRESTED IN STABBING OF OFF-DUTY NYPD DETECTIVE

The detective fought back and tried to defend himself before he was stabbed at least seven times in the neck and leg. The suspects allegedly ripped the chain from his neck and fled on a motorized bike, sources and police told the Post.

Video obtained by the newspaper showed Mercedes covered in blood as he was loaded into an ambulance after the attack. He was rushed to Jacobi Medical Center and released several days later.

Mercedes was greeted Monday evening by dozens of fellow NYPD officers as he left the hospital in a wheelchair, with bagpipes playing and officers applauding. He later stood up, smiled and flashed a thumbs-up to the crowd.

EXCLUSIVE: LEGAL GROUP TELLS NYPD COPS THEY CAN CONTACT ICE DIRECTLY DESPITE BLUE CITY'S SANCTUARY RULES

Police identified the alleged attackers as D’Angelo Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia, 24. Caraballo was identified as the alleged slasher, while Mejia was accused of driving the bike, according to the NYPD.

Both suspects were identified by federal authorities as illegal migrants from the Dominican Republic. They were found hiding in the basement of a home in Lynn, Massachusetts, and taken into custody by the U.S. Marshals Service, the NYPD said Wednesday.

The pair were ordered held without bail during a joint appearance in Lynn District Court and are expected to be returned to New York City to face attempted murder charges, according to police.
